utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. May we have the appearances now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Teresa McHenry for the Prosecution, along with Mr. Huber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I am Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Mr. Delalic is also represented by my colleague, Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DURIC
utterances.text: My name is Niko Duric and I am representing Mr. Zdravko Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I am Salih Karabdic, attorney for Mr. Hazim Delic, along with Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I am Cynthia McMurrey and along with my colleague, Ms. Nancy Boler, we represent Esad Landzo. Ms. Boler will not be present in the Courtroom today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We'll begin this morning with your next witness, Mr. Moran. I see Mrs. McHenry is standing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just wanted to advise the Court that this -- I am not now asking for anything, but I wanted to advise the Court that this is a doctor who is testifying as an expert. There has been no expert report. On Monday afternoon we received 250 pages of transcript that the doctor used to prepare, and this morning, and I had an opportunity to skim that material. This morning I got a few more pages, which I have not even had an opportunity to look at. Of course, I am not a doctor, and not having had an expert report, I haven't been able even to consult with anyone about what he may or may not say and cross-examination. I am not now asking for a continuance of the cross-examination. I am just -- because I have no idea what he is going to say, and so it may not be necessary. I just wanted to apprise the Court of the situation. So in the unfortunate event I have to ask for a continuance before cross-examination, at least you would know what the situation that the Prosecution is faced with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, just so that the record is clear, I received a letter from the Office of the Prosecutor on Monday saying that they wanted these documents by 2.30 on Monday or otherwise they would have to ask for a continuance. And those documents were provided to them, or made available to them, prior to the time that they asked for. Just so that the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is that really the issue? What is the direction here -- the directive here about presenting an expert witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, Dr. Bellas has not prepared a written report. He is basing his opinions solely on testimony of the Prosecution witnesses. Nothing more and nothing less, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What is the expertise he is expecting to give to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour -- you mean his expertise, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, what is his area of expertise, since all he is doing is to comment --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Dr. Bellas is a forensic pathologist. Is he a graduate of the medical school in, I believe, the University of Havana Cuba.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is his qualification. I am asking for the expertise you expect him to give.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I expect Dr. Bellas to testify that based on the assumption that the Prosecution witnesses were telling the truth, when they testified, that their testimony, in all reasonable medical probability, and he'll define that term for you, there would have been substantially more deaths in the camps, there would have been substantially more injuries, there would have been substantially more illness. The physical condition of the inmates at the Celebici camp, both based on lack of food, water, the living conditions that were described by the Prosecution witnesses, and the abuse that was described by the Prosecution witnesses, that if, in fact, that occurred, one would expect that there would be substantially -- there would have been much worse injuries. There would have, in all likelihood, been a severe outbreak of communicable diseases, there would have been -- one would expect that there would be substantial numbers of people suffering from heat stroke, which is a life threatening condition. That there would have been severe dehydration, possibly causing death, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: These are your own opinions, not his own -- anyway, let's carry on with him, because what you are saying is an opinion that he would give, any other person could give. Now, let's hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, Dr. Bellas has not been sworn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed, please

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Bellas.

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Would you introduce yourself to members of the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: My first name is Eduardo and last name Bellas, B-e-l-l-a-s.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, doctor, tell the members of the Trial Chamber about your formal education?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: I received my medical diploma in 1957, February. I spent two years in rotating internship in the hospital of the University of Havana Medical School for two years. Then I train three years in the field of pathology. That was between 1959, 1962, January, January. After that I was a full licensed pathologist in the island --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: When you say "the island", what island are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Cuba. This was until 1971, the last day of the year, that is on December the 30th, 1971. That day I travelled to the United States and six months later I revalidate my medical diploma in Balor Medical School at Houston that was on July 26th, 1972. Beginning in January the 1st, 1973, until the last day, January, 1974, that is two years, that time was spent with the University of Texas Medical School at Houston in training in pathology. That is the second time in my life I take training in pathology. After I finished this training, I was appointed assistant medical examiner for Harris County in Houston, Texas. I hold this position for about more than 15 years, when I was appointed deputy chief medical examiner for Harris County, Houston, Texas. The last year I spent in the office, I was acting chief medical examiner for Harris County, Houston, Texas. I belong to the basic organisations in my field, in my career, and I have licence to practice medicine in the state of Texas and in the state of Florida, both.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, while you were in Cuba, would you tell the judges about the practical experience you had, the jobs, where you worked, and what your duties were.

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: I spent, I say, full licensed pathologist in Cuba. I spent most of the time in teaching hospitals. That is, my practice in Cuba was mainly in the field of pathology in the area of the teaching hospital in the island. And that was a very active practice with many meetings and preparation of clinical pathology conferences. The practice in Cuba was predominantly in the hospital field, and the practice in the United States in the forensic area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, what are the duties of the office of the medical examiner for Harris County, Texas, in general?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: In general, we have the main duty to establish the cause of death. People under certain circumstances, we handle the cases, homicide, accidental, suicidal death, and also some type of natural causes of death under circumstances that the law establish. We have to establish the cause of death. One of our duties, also, is to help or to come to the opinion about the manner of death. We have the suicide, the homicide, the accidental death, the natural death, and sometimes, when the situation is not clear, the manner of death, we -- we come and determine. Another duty is that we are requested very, very often to testify in Court for the different cases, particularly in homicide. But that is not the only situation. There are civil litigations, there are situations of death while at work that require some opinions and some considerations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor --

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: -- about circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: About testifying, how many times have you testified as an expert witness in criminal trials?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: In the beginning I start to count them, but in a period of time of 20 years I didn't count. Several hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And how many of those were you testifying as an expert witness for the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Many, many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, you've testified as an expert witness for the Prosecutor, in, what, four murder cases where I was the Defence attorney?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Give or take. Doctor, just so that the judges will have an idea of the volume of practice, approximately how many investigations per year are conducted by the Harris County Medical Examiner's Office into the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: We were escalating from 1975 to 1996, when I stopped working for the Medical Examiner's Office. The number of homicides and other causes of death, several hundred, even in the scale of thousands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Per year?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Not per year, but in total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am just wondering --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually, the number of murders we have has gone down from about 700 a year down to, what, about 450?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: 400 homicides in the last years, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So that's -- that will give Your Honour some idea of the scale that we are talking about. And, doctor, it's not just homicides, but, for instance, you would see -- investigate deaths and trauma caused by things like traffic accidents or falls or --

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. All kinds of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And do you hold any -- are you certified by any agencies as a board certified pathologist or forensic pathologist?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes. There is the speciality board in the United States. I am certified with the American Board of Pathology. I received that in anatomical pathology in 1985, and board certification in forensic in 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you are still receiving training in both pathology and just general medicine, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: All the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, I think you just told me you just finished, what, 35 hours worth of training? Was I right on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Or some number of hours, just in the last couple of weeks.

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, doctor, because -- based on your training and your experience, are you familiar with the effects of blunt trauma on the human body?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What is blunt trauma?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Blunt trauma or blunt force are injuries that are associated with solid objects. In blunt trauma we have to distinguish two type of lesions. One is the contusion, the synonym for contusion is bruise, B-R-U-I-S-E, is the same thing. A contusion is blunt force inflicted over the surface of the body, sufficient to produce haemorrhage or extravasation. Extravasation and haemorrhage are synonyms. And, of course, under the circumstances there is swelling and discoloration, bluish-black in the beginning and later on these colours start to fade and replaced by a brown and yellow colour, until everything disappears. That is the bruise or the contusion, sufficient to produce haemorrhage, swelling, and discoloration, but not sufficient to produce tear. If there is a tear, that is a discontinuation of the tissue, rupture of the tissue, then we call laceration, blunt force. Laceration is an open door for infection. That doesn't mean that a bruise or a contusion could not be infected as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And when you say laceration, what you are saying is a cut, an opening in the skin?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: A tear of the skin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And a contusion is a bruise?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In layman's terms. And are you familiar with the infliction of blunt trauma on, for instance, a head?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And how about burns? Have you seen burns very often in your practice?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And are you familiar with the kinds of injuries that burns would cause, both in people who are living and people who are deceased?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And are you familiar with the effects of starvation, dehydration, high temperature, things like that on the human body?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And the things that that would likely to cause, both in people who are deceased and people who are still alive?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now, your practice in the last 20 years has been limited to dead people?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: But you still, based on your training and experience, both as a physician and as a medical examiner, know what would likely occur in a living person also?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, we are going to use the phrase, or I am going to use the phrase several times, the phrase "in all reasonable medical probability". Would you define what you mean by that to the judges.

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Reasonable, something that makes sense. Probability is a strong evidence that something can happen. And medical, within the medical field, medical job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And typically in your past practice, in the past times, when you've testified as an expert witness, you've had the advantage of examining the body or examining the patient and seeing lab results; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes, several, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And we didn't have that in this case?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, did I give you a volume of about 250 pages of transcripts of the testimony?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And did you base your opinion on that?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the help of the usher, I have four copies of that. One for the registry and one for each member of the Trial Chamber. I am not going to introduce it into evidence. It's nothing but excerpts from the transcript. But I want the Trial Chamber to see what he relied on. Also, Your Honour, due to a printing error, a reproduction error, the last three pages of what Dr. Bellas was given were omitted from your volumes. I will -- two or three pages. At the break I will have them reproduced and brought up. And I apologise for the reproduction error. Doctor, when I asked you to examine this, did I tell you to presume that the witnesses for the Prosecution were telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And then did I ask you to form an opinion based upon what you presumed to be truthful evidence?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: As to what, in all reasonable medical probability, would have been the results of various pieces of evidence?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, I would first like to talk you a little bit about the conditions in the camp, as described by the witnesses for the Prosecution, as to food, water, cleanliness, toilet conditions, living conditions. And tell the judges the facts you are going to base your opinion on, just describe what you understand the conditions in the Celebici camp to be as described by the witnesses for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: The conditions, in general, were, according with the transcripts, very poor conditions, very -- extremely dangerous situation for many, many complications, as infections or dehydration, high environmental temperature. In other words, multi-factoral circumstances that all of them very, very, obviously, to endanger human life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, about the environmental conditions, let's talk a little bit about temperature. As you described it, I showed you pictures of hangar 6 and given the conditions as described by the Prosecution witnesses, and the fact that other witnesses both for the Prosecution and the Defence, have described the summer of 1992 as a hot summer, what would it have been like in that hangar when you had 200, 250 people jammed in there? What would it do to temperature and humidity?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: The temperature outside is usually less than inside, particularly when there are many people crowded in one place. Under the circumstances, the people sweat more, they need more water than usual, and there is always a potential that some of the three degrees of heat related disease can come. Sometimes the first degree is exertion. The other extreme in degree that can kill is heat stroke, and in between, a situation where the high temperature, particularly when there is not sufficient water supply, can come. Exertion is, by large, the most frequent situation. Heat stroke has the potential to kill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Describe for the judges what causes heat stroke and what its effect is on the human body.

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: If the environmental temperature is too high, and if the person doesn't have adequate fluids, there is a point where the temperature control of the organism is lost. So what is established is a very, very high, uncontrollable temperature, and that temperature, after 100, 2, 3, 4, 5, 106 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's temperature Fahrenheit?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Fahrenheit, yes. Fahrenheit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That would be about how many Celcius, doctor, how many degrees Celcius?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Well, the body temperature for the human is 37 in Centigrade, but the scale, when it come 41, 40, but maintained for a certain time, then the person who is going to have heat stroke and that, the temperature is not controllable any more, that temperature, 42 or 106 in Fahrenheit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And given the amount of water that the Prosecution witnesses testified that they were given access to during the period of May, June, July, August of 1992, do you have an opinion, based on all reasonable medical probability, of the chances of heat stroke of the people being confined in hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Considering that heat stroke is a maximum expression of that -- or the result of being under high temperature, environmental high temperature and not adequate fluid supply, it's an extreme situation, but in the middle or below that to the most benign situation, exertion, because of the temperature, I would suspect under the circumstances more problems with the temperature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did you, for instance, in your practice in Houston in the Medical Examiner's Office, did you see heat stroke on occasion?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And what kinds of things would cause heat stroke -- because, before they got to you they were dead. Sufficient to cause death?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: My experience was that most of them came up working under the sun in construction areas, and those working in the attics, of course always in summer time. Those are the two more frequent cases. People in the attic, working in the attic and those working in the outside, particularly in construction, or in the fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And given the conditions in the Celebici camp, as described by the Prosecution witnesses, would you have expected to see numerous cases of heat stroke?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Well, if not numerous, I could expect to have some people with real, real problems about the environmental temperature. I would expect that, yes, more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now, let me tie this lack of water in with the sanitary conditions in the camp, as described by the Prosecution witnesses. The way they described dirty water, water with pieces of faeces in it, all sharing the same eating utensils, living -- even sitting in human waste. Would that likely cause diseases that would increase the amount of dehydration?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes, they can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What kind of diseases are we talking about, doctor?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Well, under the circumstances, infectious disease, either in the skin, particularly in the area that has been contused or lacerated, are more prone to be infected. Also, diarrhoea is another complication that you expect. And, of course, there is also all kinds of contaminations, infections, by oral way with the food.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, would this diarrhoea that you just talked about, would that have an effect on the amount of dehydration when you add it to the lack of drinking water?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes. On these circumstances diarrhoea produce some effects under ordinary circumstances, but when the circumstances are adverse, like in this case, the situation is worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Would you expect the combination of the heat and the diarrhoea, that you would expect, based on the contamination and dirty living conditions, to cause death or serious illness to those inmates?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes, because it is multi-factoral.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In all reasonable medical probability, are we talking about a substantial number of deaths based just solely on disease?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes. Situation when the life threatening conditions are very, very probable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now, if the witnesses for the Prosecution are accurately describing in the conditions in the camp, and if there were approximately 250 people in that hangar, and if you'd like I can show you pictures of the interior of the hangar, and are we talking about -- well, how many deaths, roughly, would we expect, based on dehydration and heat stroke, solely due to the lack of clean drinking water and the resulting diseases? Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Well, I cannot go on statistical data at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: But a rough estimate of the amount of people there, the circumstances that is reflected in the testimonies, that I would expect more problems, more lacerations, more infections, more gastro-intestinal disturbances, and probably more that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: By the way, doctor, I think it's in the -- I'm sure it is in the excerpts that you have. One of the witnesses for the Prosecution testified that he did not have a bowel movement for 13 days and that there were others who did not have bowel movements for 40 days while they were confined in the Celebici prison. Given the conditions as described by the Prosecution, in all reasonable medical probability, is that possible?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: The 13 days is perfectly acceptable, under the circumstances that these persons were. Forty days, I have no information of any case of forty days. But as I said before, the human body has a -- sometimes an unbelievable resistance for life. I wouldn't be reluctant to accept 40 days without bowel movement. But it would be very unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about the human body being tough. We are tough creatures. The good lord made us pretty tough. Your Honour, did you have a question? I'm sorry, I thought you had a question. But, on the other hand, sometimes, seemingly, minor things can cause serious bodily injury or death, can't they?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Sometimes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And that would vary, I suspect, somewhat on the age of the person and the general health of the person, and it would probably also -- is that correct, doctor? Am I correct in that assumption?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. We have two extremes, the elderly and the children. They are more liable than anybody else. In the middle are the most resistant people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And how about the availability of medical care? Is that --

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: It's critical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So, for instance, if there is a good trauma facility available, a person might survive an injury, where if there is little or no medical care, he might not?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Describe for the judges what you are basing your opinion on when I talk about the food supply for the inmates?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: The food supply that I read in the different testimonies are very, very negligible, very little, in terms of calories, proteins, carbohydrates and fats. Everything is very, very low. You expect that situation like this maintained for more than 30 days will produce a very significant decrease in the body weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Would it likely, standing alone, lead to death or serious illness over a period of, say, the end of May through the end of July?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Three months.

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Three months, under these circumstances, again I will expect more serious complications associated with low nutrition level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now, doctor, would you put all of this together for us, the lack of clean water, the fact that it was dirty water, the temperature, the filthy living conditions that are described by the Prosecution witnesses, the poor diet, and setting aside any allegations of trauma at all, what would you expect would be the result of confinement under the circumstances described by the witnesses for the Prosecutor over that about two- to three-month period?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Nutrition problems and infections mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What would the people look like?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Very thin, very -- people that obviously are starving.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You've seen pictures of survivors of Auschwitz?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Would they look like that?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Is that a yes, doctor?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now, let's add in some of the other things that the Prosecution witnesses talked about. They talked about -- let's start with blunt trauma. And for that I would ask that the doctor be shown Defence Exhibit, I believe it's 6-3. Doctor, you are from Cuba, and I think this has something to do with one of your national sports, so you are familiar with these things?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine, thank you. And, doctor, have you seen the results of being beaten with one of those things on the human body?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: On healthy people, people that were previously healthy?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And how many of those did you see on your autopsy table?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: I don't remember, but probably I have seen several that a baseball bat was used, and I never did know, because I have been -- I have seen many, many blunt traumas, that in all kind of circumstances, and sometimes some -- several objects have been used. But in two or three occasions the situation of baseball bat specifically was brought to my attention. Two or three blows in the head with fractured skulls.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And if someone is hit with a baseball bat, one or two or three times, not necessarily in the head, but in other parts of the body, is that likely to cause severe injury?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Severe, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And -- well, for instance, let me describe something that's in the document. I can tell you the page number. Your Honour, the page number I am going to refer to this is the page number, not of the transcript, but at the bottom of the transcript excerpts. And on page, I believe, it's 30 and 31, one of the witnesses for the Prosecution says he was hit across the back with a baseball bat about 30 times and had some broken ribs. Doctor, if someone were hit with a baseball bat across the back 30 times, how serious, in your opinion, would the injury be?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Everything depends how much force the person that is inflicting those injuries put on the bat. It's not necessary to put too much force on a baseball bat. If you take the baseball bat for it's usual part, it's not necessary to put too much force in order to inflict a serious injury. Of course, you were talking about the back. We can have 30, with more -- you can afford that but not in the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now, our back has, among other things, ribs and the spine in it?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If one were hit very hard across the back with a baseball bat, would there be a chance of injury to the spine?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: How good -- how likely would it be that there would be some injury to the spine?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Very likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And given the kinds of injuries we are talking about, what would be the likelihood of -- well, what likely would be the type of injury we are talking about? Someone in a wheelchair?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Contusions, as most of the time, baseball bat usually do not produce lacerations unless in the -- beneath the soft tissue, there is a bone, a resistant plane. In that case the laceration is very easy to be produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The skin is stretched -- the skin is stretched (Microphone, please, Your Honour)?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Exactly. In the case of the head, it's very easy to produce a laceration because the resistance of the cranium beneath is easily tear by the blow. But in other parts of the body the contusions are the predominant lesions. But the ribs, if beings hit by the baseball bat, can be fractured with relative ease.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: How about the spine?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Well, the spine is more protected than the ribs, because the ribs come lateralise and protrude more than the spine. The spine remain a little bit hidden and covered by abundant muscles around it. It's more protected. But it can be damaged and fractured too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If there were regular beatings with a baseball bat across the back by people who were in the living conditions that you've described, and the Prosecution witnesses swore were correct, if there -- if every time I went outside to urinate I got hit across the back with baseball bat a couple of times, and if it was done to everybody, every one of these 250 people, would it be likely or unlikely that someone would be unlucky enough to have a severe enough spinal injury to cause paralysis, permanent paralysis?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Well, the paralysis represent -- it can come directly or indirectly associated with a trauma, because the paralysis can come by damage to the spine, but this damage may be associated with haematomas in the spinal canal and may produce paralysis without the bone being fractured, let's say. That is the situation. But with a baseball bat, beating people in the back, or lateral chest, the most frequent complication bones are concerned, is fractured ribs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And if those fractured ribs are not treated, given the living conditions described by the witnesses for the Prosecutor, what's the likely medical outcome? Will they eventually just heal themselves or will there be internal injuries or could it vary?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: The ribs, because they usually remain in contact, the broken part, the two segment, the proximal and the distal segments usually are more or less in contact. They can heal spontaneously with time. The ribs are healed like the bones of the upper extremities faster than the bones in the lower extremities. So they can heal and many rib fractures do not require a specific orthopaedic devices. Of course, any fracture can be subject to infection, osteomyelitis. And that is another complication, post-trauma.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Could one, given the physical conditions of the camp, if there were lots of beatings like this, one would expect lots of broken bones?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And given the fact that there are lots of broken bones that are not being treated, either no medical care or poor medical care, in all reasonable medical probability how many cases -- well, how many is a big word -- would you expect to see a substantial number of cases of osteomyelitis?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Well, at least when the fracture is produced, the healing begins almost immediately. What you see is the callous, that is the point of healing is very regular and very big, mostly -- osteomyelitis is a possibility. Every time you fracture a bone, osteomyelitis might be a complication. But under the circumstances I would expect a little bit of osteomyelitis. I don't know. I cannot go on a statistical -- it's in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure. And given the number of beatings -- well, first, let me back off a second. Tell the judges the difference between what we call a simple fracture and what we call a compound fracture.

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: If somebody hit me in this arm, for instance, and the blow is sufficient to fracture my bone in the arm, let's say one only, and the two pieces of bone remained in position without any deviation either from the distal part or the proximal part, and the situation is that the bone stayed there, and the line of fracture is, say, a thin line of fracture that is there without any irregularities, we call that simple fracture. Compound fractures means that the blow brings a separation of the proximal segment with the distal segment. Then this is done at the expenses of additional injuries to the soft tissues around the bone, because after the blow you have the contraction of the muscles that come in and out or around the bone, that they will pull one side or the other and make the healing more difficult. And that's why the compound fracture sometimes require open surgery. When the fracture is not compound, the possibilities for infections are very nil, non-significant. The compound fracture are more subject to complications, particularly infections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, is it common or uncommon in the case of a compound fracture of -- pick a bone, any bone -- for the bone, my arm, if I have a compound fracture of my lower arm, would it be common or uncommon for the bone to come through the skin?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Everything depends upon the force. When you deal with motor-vehicle accidents and accidental industrial death, you can see that very, very much. They stick out from the inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure. Now, would the trauma that's -- that's described by these witnesses for the Prosecution in their testimony, would that be fairly similar to an automobile accident or an industrial accident or is it anything that --

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: In trauma, with motor-vehicle accident you have the extreme, and many, many types of trauma because the car turn over several times, because the body was thrown from the vehicle. The primary impact brings more serious lacerations and fractures. But later on secondary trauma can produce minor things. But in this type of punishment, when you put the people against a wall and you ask to raise the hands and hit in the back, you don't expect those extremely -- the bones to stick out from the body. Fractures there, a little bit deviation is possible, or the cheek to cheek approach of both parts of the bone, fine. Much, much less. The intensity is much, much less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: By the way, one question I am going to ask, because, frankly, because Judge Jan, before you came here, mentioned something about he didn't need a physician to tell him if you get hit 200 to 250 times with a baseball bat, you are going to have severe injuries. But one of the witnesses for the Prosecutor testified that by count he was hit more than 200 times with that baseball bat up and down this side of his body. In all reasonable medical probability, doctor, what would be the result of a beating like that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Could counsel just please tell me what he is referring to, what page in the doctor's material.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure. It was testimony of Mirko Dordic and I believe on the material it's on page 33 and 35. Just so the record is clear, I think Ms. McHenry may have been the lawyer that asked the question that brought about that response.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Anyhow, doctor, what kind of injuries would one expect if you were hit 200, 250 times with a baseball bat, real hard?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: This part from the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Down the side.

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: From the waist?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: From about the armpit down to about the knee.

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Well, the possibility of rib fractures is -- both sides, 270 times?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, between 200 and 250 times on one side of the body?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: On one side of the body? All on one side?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, doctor.

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Rib fractures will be expected, of course. The rest of the injuries, because it's an area that is covered by abundant muscle, particularly thigh and the -- around the waist, everything depends on the frame of the individual, of the victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: How about if he's been starving?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: And intensity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: How about if he's been starving and filthy living conditions with little or no -- with little drinking water, none of it clean?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Oh, in that case, that person, I don't think is in the position or in the situation that afford that many trauma. That is -- that would devastating for that person under that circumstance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So in all reasonable medical probability that person would not come up four years later and testify in a Court about his injuries?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: It's a very, very unlikely that a person can afford that many blows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, while I am thinking about it, when you get multiple hits with something and, as you'll recall, there is descriptions of things, other than baseball bats, that were used to hit people, there were shovel handles, pickaxes, pipes, rifle butts that the Prosecution witnesses said were used to hit them. Let me give you a hypothetical situation. That someone is hit -- is being hit with one of these objects, pick one of them, a lead pipe, a piece of pipe, and I keep hitting. Is it likely that one of the early blows would, say, fracture a rib?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Any one can do a fractured rib.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So the very first one could fracture a rib?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What would happen if I hit him on the same place, where that fractured rib was, hit him again with had a lead pipe?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Well, in that case the chances come and come and come and the greater the number of blows, the greater the chance for fractured rib, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And would -- if I fractured a rib the first time, is it possible that the second blow could cause the rib to, per chance, pierce an internal organ?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: It's very difficult to know under these circumstances which blow inflicted the fracture. But there is one thing, after the rib was fractured and more blows come to the same area, the pain will be terrible and the swelling and the inflammation and the possibilities for infection will increase tremendously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, let's talk for a second about blunt trauma caused by rifle butts. I think you described them to me yesterday, that there's a difference in the type of injury that's likely to be caused by a rifle butt, depending upon how someone is hit with it, how the rifle is used. Would you describe that to the members of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes. We are talking about rifle butts?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Not bar. You see, as you know, the lateral surface of the butt are very smooth, and sometimes the soldiers -- this is not related to my practice as a medical examiner. We have no of those cases in Houston.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me a second. Let's be up front with the members of the Trial Chamber. You served as an officer in the military of Cuba and had military training?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Is this what you are basing your opinion on?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: And seeing many news that when the people get hit, the blow that is inflicted with rifle butt, like this, lateral blow, is very different when the people or the soldier take the rifle and do like this. This one is a tremendous penetrating power and tremendous potential to produce internal damage. Although, you see not too much outside. But the other one, which is lateralised, is a more gentle, if I may say so, blow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: When you say gentle, it's not a gentle hug like you would give your child?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Exactly. Less penetrating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now, if someone were leaning up against a wall like this, or laying on the ground and were being beaten with a rifle butt, which way would it be more likely that they would be hit, if you know? If you have any kind of an opinion on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object to this. I didn't object to the previous questions, although I am not sure they are within his expertise. But I certainly don't think this is within his expertise. Which way would it be more likely that a soldier beating someone with his hands against the arm would hit it. I would object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There is substance in what she says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll just withdraw that question. The Trial Chamber can draw its own conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, if someone is beaten with a shovel or a shovel handle sufficient to break that wooden handle in the area between, say, the waist and the knees, so including the thighs, would it be likely or unlikely that one would have a broken thigh?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: It may, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And presume that the person who is being beaten was living in the conditions described by the witnesses for the Prosecution, would that make it more or less likely, that one would have a broken thigh?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Well, it's sufficient as to produce a broken thigh. Everything depends also how hard is that piece of wood, and the complexion of some victims. Because some victims are real, real strong with powerful muscles and they are protected, but there is another possibility that although you don't see too much outside, the trauma, this time of trauma that you ask me is serious, is very, very strong, it can cause internal haemorrhages that you are not able to see. That can happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Would one expect to see those kinds of injuries in people who were living in the kinds of conditions described by the witnesses for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Well, the external evidence is always there. The internal evidence, if any, be it a fracture or a haematoma inside the pelvic or the abdominal cavity, you cannot see that from the outside. For the fractures you need the x-ray.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let's talk about head injuries for a minute. When a person is beaten in the head with fists, rifle butts, electric cables, or has his head jammed into concrete, presuming it's not sufficient to just crush his head and have horrible fractures, so there is no visible wounds, or maybe just visible laceration or something like that. But we are not talking about a crushed skull. What kinds of injuries is that likely to cause?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Assuming that this is not a pure hypothetical, I just ask Defence counsel to tell me what section of the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It's a pure hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If it's a pure hypothetical, I object as to relevancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, I would recommend that the Prosecutor look at pages 120 and 124 of the documents that I gave her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, on those pages, a witness whose name is R, testified that when they arrived at the camp they were beaten?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: 120 and 124 is what my notes show, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And this witness, Witness R, describes on page 120 of the documents that you were given -- by the way, doctor, if you look behind you, you will see a model of the camp. And the wall we are talking about is that concrete retaining wall right next to the gatehouse there, if that has any effect on your opinion. And this witness, this Witness R testified about beatings, when they arrived at the camp, and he said, and I am going to skip some areas, but I'm going to read you what he said. And this is going to be on page 7683 of the official transcript -- 7683 and 84. This beating affected all parts of the body. I personally got the strongest blows at the back of my head, also in the kidney areas. The injuries inflicted by the blows with foreheads against the wall were frequently as serious as those inflicted at the back of the head because the forehead hit against the wall every time. He further describes that he fainted twice during the beatings. One of the guards "hit me with his rifle here across the head" he indicated in the record. He doesn't say exactly where it was. And he further went on to say that this lasted for about 30 -- this is on page 124 of my notes. That it went on for about 30 to 35 minutes. They were beat with objects that were at hand and at foot, boots, beaten along the genitals, to the back of the heads, hit with rifle barrels and butts, both sides. And he says, also, they were beaten with pickaxes, with shovels, any other objects that were around the camp, because there was a warehouse, and they were also beaten with chains, cables and intertwine cables. Doctor, let's just focus on the kinds of head injuries that this person described, Witness R described. If one's head is hit in a way that's not sufficient to crack the skull or fracture the skull, what happens to the bone -- excuse me, to the brain?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: The cranial cavity or the cranial cephalic complex poses a very particular field in relation to trauma. In the absence of fractures of the skull, what happen is that when there is a fracture, let's begin with a fracture, when there is a fracture upon a blow, that means that the forces has been -- most of the forces inflicted by the blunt object have dissipated in the skull, in the bone. When there is not a fracture, the blow is transmitted toward the brain producing something that you cannot see even with a microscope. Concussion of the brain. Concussion, not contusion of the brain. Contusion of the brain is like a contusion in the skin. You see the haemorrhage, you see the swelling, and you see the discoloration. Concussion means an effect of vibration inside the brain system that can cause unconsciousness or dizziness or, in some cases of blast injury, when there is a bomb that explode, the wave will produce a vibration that can kill you, blast injury. So that's what happened to the brain when there is no fracture of the skull. The forces are dissipated in the brain tissue, produces a concussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, given the description that I just read you, would it be likely or unlikely that Witness R suffered a concussion of the brain at that point?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Concussion as a rule, no question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now, if it's treated, does it -- or untreated, does that make any difference in the outcome?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: This is something that the brain put the things again in place. If not, it's because there was an exonic injury. That is another thing, acute exonic injury can kill you in very short time, in 12 hours. But if nobody was dead in the next few hours of that concussion as a rule, and that comes to the -- everything comes to the brain again, the connections between the neuron cells, they come in the normal fashion without any treatment. It's a matter of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, would trauma like that described by Witness R -- presuming it happened to several people at the same time, similar types of abuse, is it likely or unlikely that some of those people would suffer, say, a fractured skull?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: It's possible to see fractured skull. Sometimes we can see signals in the outside that we know that there is a fracture of the skull, although we don't have an x-ray. For instance, if they see that there is a swelling in the mastoid area, left or right, and there was a bluish black discoloration and swelling in the mastoid area without any contusion, without any laceration in that area, I know that there is a fracture in the right temporal bone. Likewise, if I see that there is haemorrhage coming up from the ear canals, I know, without doing the x-ray, I make the assumption that there is a fracture of the temporal bone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Given the description that Witness R gave of this abuse, would it be likely or unlikely that someone would suffer a fracture to their skull?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Both are possible, with or without fracture. All depends upon how the blow was inflicted, because if you have the head against the wall, and you hit me right in the opposite pole of that contact with the wall, the possibilities of fracture will increase. But if the blows are inflicted not in that line, then the possibilities of fracture will decrease.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, if I am hit on the back of the head and that drives my head into the wall.

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: In that case, the fracture is more likely to be produced than not. Again, the fractures can be simple or may be compound. But the question in the brain is not that the fractures are simple or compound. It's the association, internal bleeding, either by epidural haematoma or subdural haematoma that is the real, real serious complication.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, you can have a subdural haematoma even without a fracture of the skull, can't you?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Subdural haematoma may or may not be traumatic, epidural haematoma is always traumatic in origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Tell the judges what subdural and epidural haematoma are?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Well, let's say that I have a needle and I put the needle over here and trespass the scalp. After that the needle will perforate my bone. Then, after the bone is the dura matter. Between the Dura matter and the bone, normally there is not a space. When there is a fracture of the skull, the blood is accumulated between the inner surface of the bone and the outer surface of the dura. That is epidural haemorrhage or haematoma. If the needle comes and perforate the dura, then it comes to the space between the dura and the brain. That is subdural space with subdural haemorrhage or subdural haematoma. So this are the plains that occur normally. Usually the fracture of the skull produce epidural haematoma practically 100 percent of the cases the degree of the haematoma, the degree of haemorrhage depends upon the seriousness of the bomb damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Without medical treatment, what is the prognosis generally for a person who has a subdural or epidural haematoma?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: It depends upon the volume of the haematoma. The haematoma in the subdural space in particular, they can bleed spontaneously or they can bleed upon minor trauma. It's not the case of the epidural haematoma --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You said even minor trauma can cause a subdural haematoma?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: No, no. Once you produce a traumatic subdural haematoma.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I misunderstood. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Say that the subdural haematoma is of the size of three centimetres in diameter, if you are quiet, if you are in bed, that can bleed as spontaneously and be increase in the next hours, and can kill you in the next hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: This is a life threatening injury?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And it's the type of thing that requires definitive medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Well, many blows under these circumstances not producing sufficient fractures, sufficient haemorrhage in the epidural or subdural space without fracture. They can cure as spontaneously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Or they can cause death?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, given the types and amounts of injuries that you read about in the material, that's the testimony of the Prosecution witnesses, would you expect -- would you have expected to see serious head injuries?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Would you have expected to see life threatening head injuries?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: At least life threatening complications from the injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: When you say life threatening complications, would -- those would be the things --

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Either by infection or either by the consequences of the trauma.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And given the conditions in the camp and the lack of medical care, would you expect in all reasonable medical probability that there would have been a significant number of either serious injuries or deaths?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: It's a logical estimation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. One of the things Witness R said, and I will just read it to you word for word, because I am not real sure what he meant, but we'll -- he says, "I also know that --"

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I just please have the page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: 124. It's page 7690 of the transcript, lines 13 through 16. He says, "I also know that people were beaten with pickaxes, with shovels, any other objects that were around the camp."

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If someone is hit with a pickaxe, what's that likely to do to him?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: That's a trauma similar to baseball bat. The difference is that this is a little bit more flattened. It depends upon, if you put the thin portion in contact with the skin, then the penetrating effect of the blow is more serious than if you put it rather flat against --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Basically, it's a matter of physics, that the narrower the area is, the more concentrated the energy is transmitted?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now, let's change subjects for a second. Let's talk about burns. Burns caused by -- let's start with flammable liquids, gasoline. What are the general types of burns that one sees?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: There are three types of burns. The first degree burn is associated with hyperemesis, skin becomes red and swelling. The second degree burn is associated with blistering formation. Blistering formation, the blisters can be infected and release outside and usually do not pose a rather serious infection. The third degree burns is when the skin, the subcutaneous tissue, and even the muscles, and even the bones can be involved. And there is more serious consequences, mainly in the area of infection in the third degree burns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. And you can get infections in second degree burns also, can't you?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes, but they are usually superficial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. How about if one is living in absolutely filthy living conditions?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Well, the chance for infection are more prone, more possible. The possibilities, the probability of infection increases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: How about if there's no treatment?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: First and second degrees can cure as spontaneously. Third degree usually require treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: How about if there's treatment like, for instance, and I am referring to page 179 of the notes, that the treatment would be the people -- that people put tooth paste on a burn, an open burn. What would -- what's that going to do?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Toothpaste for burns, first and second, are -- they are a good choice. They relieve the pain and they reduce the inflammation at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now, if someone pours gasoline all over my legs and lights it off and it burns for, say, 15, 20, 30 seconds, in all reasonable medical probability, what kind of injuries am I going to suffer?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: That has to come up with third degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now, third degree burn, that's where the skin is charred?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue and muscles and sometimes the bone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am not objecting. I am just wondering if counsel can tell me what section he is referring to also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let's start with pages 179 through 80 of my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: This is page 180. If someone described a burn as a very bad burn, it looked like pine bark, it was black, the wound was black and covered with blood. Would that, in all likelihood, be a third degree burn?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And if a person had a third degree burn which was caused by gasoline, and was living in those horrible living conditions that the Prosecution witnesses described, and the only treatment was some ointments that were put on the wound a few days later, not immediately but a few days later, what is the result likely to be? Let's start off with, would there be infection, in all medical probability?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: The infection is automatic in third degree burns. They are infected from the beginning. If we are talking about a gasoline spread in the skin and set on fire and the skin and the subcutaneous tissue were only involved in the depth of the burn, in that case, even in this spontaneous cure can be expected. Of course, they usually and they ideally, they usually have to have treatment, medical treatment. But that can be healed if the situation of hygiene in the camp was so poor that the possibilities of infection and that healing can linger in more than the normal, is obvious. But the black discoloration and everything depends upon the mix with pulse, with pus and blood. Because they show haemorrhage very often. Of course, there is a consequence, there is some degree of scars. There is some scarring, the type of irregular scars in that area. You don't go along with a third degree burns, you don't go without a scar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Significant scarring?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Well, depends upon the depth and the area taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Would the type of medical treatment I received influence the amount of scarring? For instance, if I were in -- pick a great burn centre hospital in America. The one you'd want to go to. If I were in that hospital with third degree burns like that, and I received skin grafting, would that create a difference in the healing and the chance of infection than if I did not have skin grafts?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And if I did not have skin grafts over that third degree burn, if I essentially had no medical treatment, in filthy conditions, would the scar, in all reasonable medical probability, be more massive or less massive?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Well, the skin graft has to do with the aesthetic problem. The skin graft doesn't have to do with the healing. It's an aesthetic consideration. The degree of scarring is a function of the -- how large is the wound and how deep it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, if it's deep enough that --

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Delayed treatment brings more damage to the tissue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. How about no treatment?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: No treatment brings more chance for infection, more damage to the tissue, and if the third degree burn is, for instance, one inch by half an inch in the beginning, without treatment, it can come to become a bigger area, because the infection that settle there, therein, will amplify the tissue damage. And the scarring is more irregular and bigger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And thinking of infection, in all reasonable medical probability, if someone poured gasoline all over my legs and set it on fire, and the wound was -- there was yellow liquid pouring from my leg, that's page 171, and other people said that -- well, given that, and given the living conditions that were described by the witnesses for the Prosecution, given the amount of food, the amount of water, the cleanliness of the water that were described by the witnesses of the Prosecution, is it, in all reasonable medical probability, likely or unlikely that a serious infection would develop?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Under these circumstances, general condition of the body is poor and the healing process will be poor too. If those things are poor, the infections take over with more intensity and more facility. It's easier for the infection to be produced. Of course, there are people that have particular resistance to infections and they react very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: But they are lucky?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes. That is why one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Unlucky to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Unlucky to begin with but lucky later or blessed, I guess may be a better word, later in the healing process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, would it be likely or unlikely that one of these infections could get out of control?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Third degree burns, superficial, usually they are under control. Without treatment and without general conditions of the entire health, any infection can come out of control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And if an infection like that gets out of control and there is no medical treatment, what likely occurs?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Well, most of the infections, complications that they bring, the dangers is mainly in the lung, pneumonia is one of the complications that they bring. Not the only one, but there are many.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And untreated pneumonia in a person in his sixties, what's --

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: That prognosis is very, very serious prognosis, life threatening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: How about gangrene?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Gangrene is another possibility that -- particularly in the lower extremities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And if gangrene develops?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Well, you begin to lose the leg and later on the life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, this might be a good time to take a break, if it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me get this from the doctor. How long does it take an open wound to develop gangrene?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Judge, that depends upon if the wound has an anaerobic micro-organism from the beginning. If the wound is associated with an anaerobic micro-organism, then that process can start with the wound at the same time. You don't see the consequences, but if you are -- later, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: When does it really manifest itself? Because it has a manifestation period. When does that notice that a wound has --

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: There may be a time period where the manifestation of the gangrene is not catch by the naked eye. That is possible. But that is very, very variable, because the different people behave different in fighting back infections. It's very variable. It depends upon how was the wound, how dirty was the wound, how deep was the wound, and the aggressivity of the micro-organism responsible for the gangrene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is it usual to observe that visibly within the first one week?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any injury is common to that stage. One can see it?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. If the person is a diabetic, that situation will come up more obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That's a precondition.

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Exactly. Exactly. You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the break, can I follow up your question just a little bit, a couple of minutes? It might be helpful and then we can have our break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, on gangrene, if I have an injury to my lower leg, and gangrene develops, first thing, how long would it be in all likelihood that I would start noticing it, if there were no medical care?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are asking a different question. The Trial Chamber will now rise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed, Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, first is a matter of housekeeping. I had left some pages out of your volumes, just by -- of those volumes. And with the help of the registry and the usher, I have four copies that can just be added to the back of the book. They replace pages 248 through the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We have been grateful for some good indexing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. It's -- I don't have my secretary here and, frankly, I thought I was pretty good with the computer and a word processing system, and I found out I am really not. It took some of the wind out of my sails about my computer experience and my computer skills, and I will apologise for that. One other housekeeping matter that the Defence lawyers have asked me to bring to the Court's attention. The clock behind me shows an incorrect time, and the guards and security people, when they are handling the accused, operate on the correct time. So, basically, the break that the Trial Chamber took was, from the accused's standpoint, about ten minutes shorter than you intended. So it made it difficult for them, especially given the -- two of them have to change floors in this building --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we'll correct it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I just wanted to bring it to your attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, right before we broke, there was some discussion about gangrene and how long it would take for it to appear. And I'd like to follow that up just a little bit. If I were to have a wound similar to the one that was described with the -- looking like pine bark and that type of thing caused by gasoline, and I were living in the living conditions similar to those that were described by the witnesses for the Prosecution, and if there was no medical care, about how long, in your estimation, would it be before the first signs of gangrene started? I know it will vary from person to person, but --

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: It's difficult to say, because everything depends on the tissues destruction, the degree of infection from the beginning, because not only those micro-organism producing gangrene are present, there are always present. And sometimes the presence of several micro-organism, one counter arrest the other. So -- but the main thing is that the situation require treatment, the sooner the better. But it requires a few hours or perhaps one day or more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If there's no treatment or no -- or very little treatment, what are we going to start seeing? Are we going to start seeing the leg discolour, are we going to smell things, are we going to -- what physical manifestations would I and people around me be able to see?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: The situations, the infection can go through without gangrene and it may come with gangrene. If there is a gangrene, the gangrene, the micro-organism works very fast. It is very significant. And then you have the discoloration, the tissue is coming black little by little. And when the tissue is black, it's because there is death of that tissue. We call that necrosis. And the infection ensue into the area, later on to the region, to the whole leg, and if you don't cut the leg on time, then life is next.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, doctor, if -- again using our gasoline example. Is there a difference in the kinds of burns if the gasoline is poured directly on my skin or if the gasoline is poured on my pant leg?

utterances.speaker: EDUARDO BELLAS
utterances.text: Yes, there is a difference, because the gasoline normally is a volatile substance. We all know that. But if you pour on the clothes, and the clothes get wet for a longer period of time, the longer the contact, the more the chances to infiltrate the skin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, doctor, let me -- and for the benefit of the Prosecution, we are looking at pages 176 to 77, I believe. We have some testimony from a man named Nedeljko Draganic, and he describes that -- and both on pages 173 and 176 and 77, describes the -- that gasoline was poured on his pants, it was set on fire, both his legs were burned, not allowed to put out the fire, and the fire was sufficient that both of his trouser legs -- "My trouser legs were completely burnt out, both my legs had burnt."
